title: Tool Design Economics & Progressive Disclosure
summary: Every tool schema you register is paid for on every single call, whether the model uses it or not. Progressive disclosure means the model only sees a tool's full definition when it's actually about to use it.
whyItMatters: Tab 1's exercise showed the per-call tax of a handful of tools. At real scale (dozens of MCP servers, hundreds of tools) that tax alone can exceed the cost of the actual work being done.

concepts.heading: Minimize the tool surface, not just the schema verbosity
concepts.body: Fewer, more general tools (e.g. one `run_query` tool with parameters) usually beat many narrow tools (`get_user`, `get_order`, `get_invoice`, ...) for token cost, provided the model can still express the same range of actions. Consolidation is the first lever, before optimizing individual schema wording.

concepts.heading: Progressive disclosure: show a menu, not a manual
concepts.body: Instead of sending full input_schema for every tool on every call, send a short list of tool names + one-line descriptions upfront, and only expand a tool's full schema into context when the model signals intent to use it (a two-step call, or a dedicated 'get tool details' meta-tool). This is the same principle behind Claude Code's Skills: full detail loaded only on demand.

concepts.heading: Namespacing and grouping reduce cognitive and token load together
concepts.body: Grouping related tools under a shared prefix (`db.query`, `db.insert`, `slack.post_message`) helps the model pick faster and lets you disclose by group rather than by individual tool -- 'load all db.* tool schemas' is one disclosure decision instead of many.

exercises.title: Convert an always-loaded tool list into a two-step progressive disclosure pattern
exercises.goal: Measure the token savings from sending short tool summaries by default and only expanding full schemas for tools the model actually intends to use.
steps: Build a Strands agent with your real tools (5-10 of them) registered normally and record its per-call input tokens as the baseline (reuse the native-token-count pattern from Tab 1).

Build a 'catalog' meta-tool whose description lists all available tool names and one-line summaries, plus a single `call_tool(name, arguments)` dispatch meta-tool that looks up the named function and invokes it directly.

Register only the two meta-tools with the agent -- never register the real tools' schemas at all. → Expect: fixed per-call token cost proportional to two small meta-tool schemas plus one line per catalog entry, not tool count x full schema size.

Run a task that needs one of the underlying tools. → Expect: the model calls list_available_tools, then call_tool(name=..., arguments=...) -- the full input_schema of search_orders or issue_refund is never sent to the model at any point, since call_tool's own schema (name: str, arguments: dict) is all that's ever transmitted.
exercises.costImpact: For a 50-tool agent where each full schema averages 300 tokens, registering all 50 directly costs ~15,000 tokens/call fixed. The catalog + call_tool dispatch pattern costs roughly 300-500 tokens/call total, regardless of how many underlying tools exist, since only the two meta-tool schemas are ever transmitted -- the real tools' schemas never enter the model's context at all.

sources.title: Anthropic — Claude Code Skills (progressive disclosure pattern)
sources.claim: Skills load only on demand rather than being always present in context -- the source pattern this tab's technique generalizes from Claude Code to custom agent tool design.

sources.title: Anthropic — Building effective agents (tool design section)
sources.claim: Tool design as a first-class engineering concern, including keeping tool surfaces minimal and well-documented.

sources.title: Strands Agents — Agent API reference (tools parameter)
sources.claim: The @tool decorator and the tools constructor parameter accepting a list of registered functions -- the basis for keeping only meta-tools registered directly with the agent.
